voice.tone: Precise and mechanism-first: it explains how the thing works rather than how good it is, piling on dependent clauses until the reasoning is complete. No superlatives, no hype, and a built-in habit of naming its own limits in the same breath as its claims.
voice.rhythm: Long, multi-clause sentences stitched with em-dashes, colons and serial lists that unpack an idea fully before stopping — alternating with short, flat declarative sentences for scope and limits ('It does not send emails, publish campaigns or guarantee opens, clicks, revenue or conversions.'). Paragraphs each carry one idea through to its end rather than teasing several.
voice.person: Third person about the product ('MarketingOS reads...', 'it also reads...'), second person when instructing the user ('You point it at your website...'); no first-person 'I' or 'we' voice appears in the material.
exemplars: MarketingOS reads your material into a set of facts it is allowed to claim, decides what the campaign says and in what order, writes each email, has every draft read by someone who knows nothing about your product, rewrites what did not land, and hands you finished reviewed email text you can copy and paste after checking the facts, links and brand voice. Incomplete runs retain their delivery count and the reason they need attention.

It also reads the market you are being compared in — who the buyer is really deciding between, what each of them promises, which of your claims are yours alone and which make you invisible, and whether anybody on the open web has ever vouched for you. That half is not a side feature: copy can be true, well-shaped and grounded in your own material and still be interchangeable with everybody else's, and nothing a company publishes about itself can tell it which of its claims the whole category is also making.

And it reads the demand: who would actually buy this, which is not the same question as who the company says it sells to. A company's own material can only ever return the audience it already believes in — it was written by people who have been staring at their own product for years, and it names the customer they set out to have.

Each one comes back with an estimated hit rate and the reasoning behind it, and any of them can be handed to a campaign as the person every draft is written to and graded by. Pick one and it will go and find them by name, reading each organisation's own pages for a published way in — and keeping only the contact details that were actually on a page it fetched, because a fluent guess at an email address is indistinguishable from a real one until the mail bounces.

The current pilot asks existing invited users to test one real offer and share the phrases they would keep or rewrite, plus factual errors and time spent editing. E-commerce products, SaaS and other offers are supported as inputs; quality for every sector has not been established. A generation can take several minutes.

segments.name: a solo SaaS founder who still writes his own onboarding emails, badly, late at night
segments.situation: The product ships and the signup form works; what happens in the week after a signup is three emails he wrote in a hurry at launch and has not touched since. If the material is representative of who the company built this for, his week is spent on the product itself — support, a billing bug, one customer call — and marketing is the thing that moves to the weekend and then to next month. The likely pattern is a drafts folder with two half-written sequences, a chat window with an AI prompt he rewrote four times and abandoned because the output read like a press release about someone else's product, and a mailing tool already paid for and mostly empty. Hiring a copywriter has probably been priced at least once and parked: not because it is unaffordable in principle, but because the brief is the work — explaining the product well enough for a stranger to write about it feels like the same evening he does not have. None of this is reported by a buyer; it is the situation the product's own framing implies, and it should be read as a hypothesis about the week, not as something he said.

She has a real campaign she needs anyway, which is why she said yes; the risk she is carrying is that she spends an evening on a run, gets drafts that are 70% right, and the editing takes longer than writing from scratch would have — at which point she has lost the evening and owes an awkward reply. She has no price in front of her, so she cannot be evaluating this as a purchase; she is evaluating whether it earns a place in the next campaign. A single generation takes several minutes, so the loop is not interactive: she sets a run going, goes elsewhere, and comes back to judge a finished artefact she cannot nudge mid-flight.

objections.objection: I cannot actually buy this. Public registration is closed and accounts are handed out by the founder, so no matter how well the copy works on me, the only available action is to ask a stranger for a favour.
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence removes this for an uninvited reader — it confirms it. E15 states public registration is closed and E16 gives a sign-in URL that only works for people who already have an account. The only honest copy to a non-invited reader asks to be let in, not to buy; the only honest campaign audience right now is people who already have accounts.

objections.objection: There is no price. I cannot tell whether this is £20 a month or £2,000, I cannot get it approved, and a subscription with an unpublished price reads like 'expensive' or like 'not finished'.
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence answers this. The material explicitly states that no public subscription price is established, and there are no plans to quote. This objection cannot be beaten with what we currently know; copy must not imply affordability, trial terms, or that a price exists somewhere.

objections.objection: There is no proof it works. No customer has said anything, there are no results, and the product states outright that it will not guarantee opens, clicks, revenue or conversions. I am being asked to trust a description.
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence answers this, and pretending otherwise is the fastest way to lose a sceptical reader. There are no testimonials, no case studies and no performance results; E20 is a refusal to guarantee outcomes, not a reassurance. The only available honest substitute is the mechanism itself — a cold reader reviews every draft and what did not land is rewritten (E3) — and a mechanism is not evidence of a result. Treat the absence as a fact to be stated, not papered over.

objections.objection: I already do this with ChatGPT for free. I paste my landing page in, ask for five onboarding emails, and get five onboarding emails in thirty seconds instead of several minutes.
objections.answer: Partially answerable on mechanism, not on outcome. What the evidence supports: the material is compiled into a set of facts the writer is allowed to claim, every draft is read by a reviewer with no product knowledge and what did not land is rewritten (E3); the competitive read tells you which of your claims the whole category is also making, which nothing in your own material can (E5); audience research returns buyers your material could not contain, each with a hit rate and reasoning, and any of them can be made the person every draft is graded against (E8). None of that is a single prompt. What the evidence cannot claim is that the result is better — nobody has measured it.

objections.objection: It does not send. So I still open my mailing tool, rebuild the sequence, re-check every fact and link and the brand voice myself — this adds a step to my week and removes none of the responsibility.
objections.answer: Half answerable, and the half that is not should be said plainly. The evidence is explicit that the application drafts only and the user reviews and transfers the text into their own sending tool (E19), and that it does not send or publish (E20). What it does carry across is finished output in the shape the sending tool needs — subject, preview, body, call to action, with text copy/export and an HTML preview (E18) — and drafts that have already been through a cold-reader review and rewrite rather than first drafts (E3). The checking stays with the reader; copy that implies otherwise will be contradicted by the first run.

objections.objection: It will invent things about my product. A confident wrong sentence in front of my own list costs me more than an empty campaign, and I will have to read every line anyway — so where is the saving?
objections.answer: Answerable on design, not on a track record. The pipeline compiles the supplied material into a set of facts it is allowed to claim before writing (E3), and the contact-finding pass keeps only details that were actually on a page it fetched, on the stated reasoning that a fluent guess at an email address is indistinguishable from a real one until the mail bounces (E9) — the same posture applied to facts. The honest limit: the handover explicitly expects the user to check facts, links and brand voice (E19), and the pilot asks users to report factual errors (E21), which concedes that errors occur.

objections.objection: Quality has not been established for my sector. I am not interested in being the experiment that finds out — on a real offer, with a real list, on my name.
objections.answer: Only answerable by naming it. The material itself states that e-commerce, SaaS and other offers are supported as inputs but that quality for every sector has not been established (E22), and the current pilot is precisely an invitation to find out on one real offer and report back what to keep, what to rewrite and how long the editing took (E21). The correct offer to this person is a bounded test on one campaign, not a claim of reliability.

objections.objection: Finding named people by reading organisations' pages sounds like scraping. I am not putting my brand on a list someone built off other companies' websites, and my legal review would ask questions I cannot answer.
objections.answer: Partially answerable. The evidence states contacts come from reading each organisation's own pages for a published way in, and that only contact details actually present on a fetched page are kept rather than guessed addresses (E9); and the application does not send emails or messages on the user's behalf (E13, E20), so nothing leaves without the user's own tool and consent. The evidence says nothing about jurisdictions, consent bases or retention, so copy must not reassure on compliance.

objections.objection: We already have a sequence, and templates in our mailing tool. 'Not perfect' is not a reason to introduce a new tool, a new login and a new thing to explain to whoever covers for me.
objections.answer: Weakly answerable, and only against the sameness argument rather than the switching cost. The strongest available line is that an existing sequence can be entirely true, well-shaped and grounded in your own material and still be interchangeable with every competitor's (E5), and that your own material can only return the audience you already believe in (E6) — neither of which proofreading or reusing templates can surface. Nothing in the evidence addresses migration effort, team handover or cost of adoption.

objections.objection: A run takes several minutes and I cannot steer it while it runs. If the brief was slightly wrong I pay the full wait again to find out, and my actual working rhythm is twenty minutes between interruptions.
objections.answer: Thinly answerable. The material states plainly that a generation can take several minutes (E23) — it is disclosed, not hidden — and incomplete runs retain their delivery count and the reason they need attention, so a run that fails partway is resumable context rather than a blank restart (E4). There is no evidence about retry cost or how often briefs need a second pass.

objections.objection: I would rather pay a copywriter who learns my product once and stays. A person asks me questions, takes a brand voice note and owns the outcome; software hands me text and owns nothing.
objections.answer: Only partly answerable, and not on ownership — the product explicitly guarantees no outcome (E20). What the evidence offers against the copywriter is the brief: the input is your website, a PDF or a screenshot plus a request in your own words (E2), rather than a kickoff call and a voice document; and the cold-reader review and rewrite (E3) is the part a solo copywriter usually does not have. Accountability for the result stays with the reader either way, and copy should not claim otherwise.

objections.objection: This is not for a team our size. We have a copywriter, a brand voice guide and a review process; a tool that drafts emails from our website solves a problem we no longer have.
objections.answer: Answerable by moving the value off drafting. The research half is not addressed to the drafting bottleneck: who the buyer is really deciding between, which of your claims are yours alone, and whether anyone on the open web has vouched for you (E5), plus a demand pass returning buyers your own material could not contain, each with an estimated hit rate and reasoning (E6, E7, E8). Those remain open questions for a team that already writes well. No evidence exists for multi-seat use, review workflow or brand-guide ingestion, so copy must not imply team features.

objections.objection: The company behind this used to be something else — an agent builder with a Slack bot and credits. If the product changed shape once, the thing I learn this quarter may not exist next quarter.
objections.answer: Weakly answerable, and only by being specific about what this product is now: an email campaign drafting and market-research application (E14), in a private pilot provisioned by the founder with public registration closed (E15). The prior product's claims are explicitly out of scope. Nothing in the evidence speaks to the company's longevity, funding or roadmap, so no reassurance about continuity can be offered.

gaps.question: What does it cost, and is there a free trial or free tier?
